**Looking for an open‑source Notion replacement?** Below are three projects that are actively maintained, self‑hostable, and cover the core Notion capabilities (documents, databases, kanban, markdown, AI‑assisted writing, and data ownership).  

---

### 1. **AppFlowy** – “Open‑source Notion alternative with self‑hosted data”
- **Fit:** Full‑featured workspace with rich‑text docs, relational databases, kanban, calendar, AI writers, and offline mode.  
- **Strengths**
  - Real‑time collaboration, multiple view types (grid, board, calendar, list) and powerful import/export tools【0†L26-L31】.  
  - AGPL‑3.0 licensed, free to self‑host; Docker, Flatpak, Snap, and native installers are provided【0†L31-L34】.  
  - Extremely active development – latest commit today, 13 releases in the last 90 days【0†L43-L45】.  
- **Trade‑offs**
  - Some advanced Notion features (e.g., timeline, map view) are still a work‑in‑progress.  
  - The UI is still maturing compared with the polished Notion SaaS experience.  
- **Links**: [Website](https://appflowy.com) • [GitHub repo](https://github.com/AppFlowy-IO/AppFlowy) • [Feature comparison](https://appflowy.com/compare/notion-vs-appflowy)  

---

### 2. **AFFiNE** – “Notion + Miro, local‑first knowledge base”
- **Fit:** Combines docs, whiteboard‑style canvases, relational databases, and AI tools in a single workspace.  
- **Strengths**
  - MIT‑licensed core; free for up to 10 seats, with optional paid Pro plan for larger teams【2†L412-L419】.  
  - Supports databases, kanban, galleries, timelines, AI‑assisted writing, and a unified “knowledge‑base” view【2†L426-L433】.  
  - Very active (daily commits, dozens of releases in the past 90 days)【0†L46-L48】.  
- **Trade‑offs**
  - The free tier is limited to 10 users; larger teams need a paid plan.  
  - The UI is still evolving; some users may prefer a more classic Notion‑style layout.  
- **Links**: [Website](https://affine.pro) • [GitHub repo](https://github.com/toeverything/AFFiNE) • [Feature overview](https://affine.pro)  

---

### 3. **HedgeDoc** – “Collaborative markdown notes (like Notion’s plain‑text side)”
- **Fit:** Ideal if you mainly need lightweight, markdown‑focused docs with real‑time collaboration.  
- **Strengths**
  - AGPL‑3.0 licensed, easy to self‑host via Docker, Snap, or native packages【0†L31-L33】.  
  - Actively maintained (last commit 14 days ago, recent releases)【0†L43-L45】.  
  - Simple UI, good for meeting notes, wikis, and technical documentation.  
- **Trade‑offs**
  - Lacks the rich database, kanban, and advanced page‑layout features of Notion.  
  - No built‑in AI or visual whiteboard capabilities.  
- **Links**: [Website](https://hedgedoc.org) • [GitHub repo](https://github.com/hedgedoc/hedgedoc)  

---

#### Quick decision guide
| Need | Best fit |
|------|----------|
| Full Notion‑style docs + databases + kanban + AI + self‑host | **AppFlowy** |
| Integrated whiteboard/visual canvas + docs + databases + local‑first + optional paid tier | **AFFiNE** |
| Simple markdown collaborative notes (no databases/kanban) | **HedgeDoc** |

All three projects are open source, can be self‑hosted, and have recent activity, making them reliable alternatives to Notion. Choose the one that aligns best with the feature set and team size you require.

L76: documents, wikis, project management, databases, AI capabilities, and workspace
L77: management features that cover the majority of workflows teams use Notion for
L78: today. AppFlowy offers capabilities that many organizations require but cannot
L79: achieve with Notion, including self-hosting, deployment flexibility, local and
L80: on-prem AI, infrastructure ownership, offline workspace, and deep customization.
L81: AppFlowy's database system has evolved rapidly and now includes advanced filters,
L82: two-way relations, rollups, calculations, templates, and multiple database views.
L83: Combined with a rich-text editor that supports 40+ content types, AppFlowy can
L84: support a wide range of knowledge management and operational workflows.
L85: Organizations that rely heavily on Notion's most advanced ecosystem integrations
L86: or specific database views such as Timeline and Map views may still find
L87: limitations today, but AppFlowy continues to close that gap with every release.
L88: 
L89: ### Can I run AI locally in AppFlowy? Can I run AI locally in Notion?
L90: 
L91: Yes, you can run local AI via Ollama or LMStudio in AppFlowy. This flexibility is
L92: especially valuable for organizations with security, compliance, or data
L93: residency requirements. Notion AI, by contrast, currently relies on third-party,
L94: cloud-hosted AI services and does not support running AI models locally on your
L95: own infrastructure. AppFlowy allows organizations to connect local and
L96: self-hosted AI models, enabling AI-powered workflows without sending sensitive
L97: information to external providers. Teams can choose the AI models they use, where
L98: those models run, and whether AI features are enabled at all.

L100: ### What unique AI features does AppFlowy offer that Notion doesn't support?
L101: 
L102: Vault Workspace is a special AI workspace type that Notion doesn't support. It
L103: provides a full-featured AI that runs entirely on your device, a rich-text editor
L104: that supports 40+ content types and database views for organizing information,
L105: and local AI search that answers questions fully offline without a single byte
L106: leaving your vault. It is designed for professionals, such as portfolio managers,
L107: healthcare consultants, and high-tech research scientists, who need maximum
L108: control over sensitive data. This combination of local storage, offline access,
L109: and locally running AI provides a level of privacy and data ownership that is
L110: difficult to achieve with traditional cloud-first workspace platforms. Notion
L111: does not offer an equivalent workspace type that combines local data storage with
L112: support for locally hosted AI models.

L114: ### How do AppFlowy's databases compare to Notion's?

L121: and Sorting options, Linked views of data source, Multi-row bulk actions. For

L282: # Installing on Linux
L283: 
L284: AppFlowy currently does not have a formal Linux installation process. However,
L285: the application can quickly and easily be installed by the end user.
L286: 
L287: Note: AppFlowy requires glibc >= 2.32 however this version is not yet available
L288: in some common linux distributions. For the record, glibc 2.33 is available on
L289: Debian testing and Ubuntu 21.04:
L290: 
L291: Note: The following steps have been verified on the following Linux
L292: distributions:
L293: 
L294: - \[x\] lubuntu 20.04 - x86\_64
L295: 
L296: - \[x\] Arch Linux - x86\_64
L297: 
L298: - \[x\] Ubuntu 20.04 - x86\_64
L299: 
L300: - \[x\] Linux Mint 20.3 x86\_64
L301: 
L302: Any Linux distribution not listed here has not been tested, and the following
L303: steps may not work. If you are trying to install AppFlowy on a Linux distribution
L304: not listed here, let us know how it went so that we can add it to the list or fix
L305: any bugs that may occur.
L306: 
L307: ### Steps to install AppFlowy on Linux
L308: 
L309: 1. Download the latest archive file from the Releases page.
L310: 
L311: 2. Extract the archive in a location of your choice (e.g. `/opt/`).
L312: 
L313: note: Performing read/write operations in folders such as `/opt` may require root
L314: access. If a command fails due to missing permissions, try running it as the root
L315: user (this may be done by switching to the root user or using programs such as
L316: sudo and doas).
L317: 
L318: note: The application will be extracted into a folder named AppFlowy.
L319: 
L320: ```shell
L321: tar -xzvf AppFlowy-linux-x86.tar.gz
L322: 
L323: ```
L324: 
L325: 1. Go to the AppFlowy directory.
L326: 
L327: ```shell
L328: cd AppFlowy
L329: 
L330: ```
L331: 
L332: 1. Run the application.
L333: 
L334: ```shell
L335: ./app_flowy
L336: 
L337: ```
L338: 
L339: ### Emoji Font Installation
L340: 
L341: AppFlowy will look for the Noto Color Emoji font on your system when trying to
L342: display emoji unicode characters. Please make sure that the font is configured so
L343: that emoji characters are displayed correctly.
L344: 
L345: note: Certain distributions (e.g. Fedora Linux) already have this set up by
L346: default. In that case, you can safely ignore this section.
L347: 
L348: 1. Install the the font:
L349: 
L350: - On Arch and Manjaro Linux, install `noto-fonts-emoji` using pacman.
L351: 
L352: - On Ubuntu Linux and Linux Mint, install `fonts-noto-color-emoji` using apt.
L353: 
L354: 1. Configure the font:
L355: 
L356: - First, run `fc-cache -v` to reload the system font cache.
L357: 
L358: - Then, create a file in `/etc/fonts/local.conf` with root privileges or
L359: `~/.config/fontconfig/fonts.conf` with the following content:
L360: 
L361: ```
L362: <?xml version="1.0"?>
L363: <!DOCTYPE fontconfig SYSTEM "fonts.dtd">
L364: <fontconfig>
L365: <alias>
L366: <family>sans-serif</family>
L367: <prefer>

L452: # Installing & Setting up Flutter on Linux from Source
L453: 
L454: This guide provides step-by-step instructions to install and set up Flutter on
L455: Linux from source. It is primarily targeted at Debian-based distributions but
L456: should work for the majority of them.
L457: 
L458: Update your system by running the following command:
L459: 
L460: ```shell
L461: sudo apt update
L462: 
L463: ```
L464: 
L465: Install the necessary packages using the command:
L466: 
L467: ```shell
L468: sudo apt install curl file git unzip xz-utils zip libglu1-mesa clang cmake \
L469: ninja-build pkg-config libgtk-3-dev
L470: 
L471: ```
L472: 
L473: Optionally, you can choose to install cmake and ninja-build from source. This
L474: step is not recommended but provided for advanced users. You can download cmake
L475: from here and ninja-build from here. Note that installing cmake is required to
L476: install ninja-build or Python.
L477: 
L478: Create a new folder for Flutter by running the following command:
L479: 
L480: ```shell
L481: mkdir projectfolder
L482: 
L483: ```
L484: 
L485: Download the latest Flutter SDK tarball file
L486: 
L487: ## Installation
L488: 
L489: Change into the project folder you created earlier:
L490: 
L491: ```shell
L492: cd projectfolder
L493: 
L494: ```
L495: 
L496: Extract the Flutter tarball file using the command:
L497: 
L498: ```shell
L499: tar xvf ~/Downloads/flutter_linux_*-stable.tar.xz
L500: 
L501: ```
L502: 
L503: Add Flutter to your environment PATH by executing the following command:
L504: 
L505: ```shell
L506: export PATH="$PATH:[path-to-flutter-directory]/bin"
L507: 
L508: ```
L509: 
L510: Optionally, you can add the PATH by opening the .bashrc file using the command:
L511: 
L512: ```shell
L513: nano ~/.bashrc
L514: 
L515: ```
L516: 
L517: Add the PATH configuration there.
L518: 
L519: Replace \[path-to-flutter-directory\] in the above command with the actual path
L520: to the folder where you extracted the Flutter SDK. For example, if you extracted
L521: Flutter in a folder called projectfolder, the command will be:
L522: 
L523: ```shell
L524: export PATH="$PATH:~/projectfolder/flutter/bin"
L525: 
L526: ```
L527: 
L528: Save the file by pressing Ctrl+O and then Ctrl+X.
L529: 
L530: ### Reload Terminal Session
L531: 
L532: Reload your terminal session by either reopening the terminal or running the
L533: following command:
L534: 
L535: ```shell
L536: /bin/bash
L537: 
L538: ```
L539: 
L540: Check if the Flutter PATH is correctly added to your shell by running:
L541: 
L542: ```shell
L543: echo $PATH
L544: 
L545: ```
L546: 
L547: Once you have confirmed that Flutter is installed and the PATH is set, run the
L548: following command to check the Flutter version:
L549: 
L550: ```shell
L551: flutter --version
L552: 
L553: ```
L554: 
L555: You should see a welcome screen along with the installed version of Flutter.

L557: # Docker
L558: 
L559: A simple way of running AppFlowy is with the use of a Docker container. And we
L560: have one for you at Docker Hub!
L561: 
L562: ```
L563: docker run --rm \
L564: -v $HOME/.Xauthority:/root/.Xauthority:rw \
L565: -v /tmp/.X11-unix:/tmp/.X11-unix \
L566: -v /dev/dri:/dev/dri \
L567: -v /var/run/dbus/system_bus_socket:/var/run/dbus/system_bus_socket \
L568: -v appflowy-data:/home/appflowy \
L569: -e DISPLAY=${DISPLAY} \
L570: appflowyio/appflowy_client:main
L571: 
L572: ```
L573: 
L574: Using the `main` tag you will run the latest Appflowy version (from the `main`
L575: branch). You can also use specific releases using the tags (such as `0.0.5.3`).
L576: Check out the available tags.
L577: 
L578: Note: Appflowy inside docker needs access to your X server. In case of lack of
L579: permissions, it's recommended to build the docker image yourself. The least
L580: recommended option is running `xhost +` before running the container, but this
L581: command is considered dangerous! So make sure you run `xhost -` after it.
L582: 
L583: ## Building the docker image
L584: 
L585: ## First thing to do
L586: 
L587: Make sure you already have Docker and docker-compose fully working before
L588: attempting this procedure.
L589: 
L590: For more information, check out:
L591: 
L592: - Docker official documentation
L593: 
L594: - Docker Arch linux docs
L595: 
L596: In order to run Docker without `sudo` you must add your username to the docker
L597: group. To do this use the following command and then logout and login for it to
L598: take effect.
L599: 
L600: ```bash
L601: sudo usermod -aG docker yourusername
L602: 
L603: ```
L604: 
L605: ## Building without cloning the repository
L606: 
L607: There is no need to clone the whole repository. You can simply create a directory
L608: and download the required Docker files into that directory.
L609: 
L610: ```bash
L611: wget
L612: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AppFlowy-IO/appflowy/main/frontend/scripts/docker-buildfiles/Dockerfile
L613: wget
L614: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AppFlowy-IO/appflowy/main/frontend/scripts/docker-buildfiles/docker-compose.yml
L615: 
L616: ```
L617: 
L618: Now you are ready to build the docker image (this can take some time)
L619: 
L620: ```bash
L621: docker-compose build --build-arg uid=$(id -u) --build-arg gid=$(id -g)
L622: 
L623: ```
L624: 
L625: Lastly, run the docker container
L626: 
L627: ```bash
L628: docker-compose up
L629: 
L630: ```
L631: 
L632: ## Building with the repository installed
L633: 
L634: If you already have the repository installed then you're halfway there!
L635: 
L636: ```bash
L637: cd ./frontend/scripts/docker-buildfiles
L638: docker-compose build --build-arg uid=$(id -u) --build-arg gid=$(id -g)
L639: 
L640: ```
L641: 
L642: Lastly, run the docker container
L643: 
L644: ```
L645: docker-compose up
L646: 
L647: ```

L734: # AppFlowy Mentorship Program

L736: # Program Guidance
L737: 
L738: ## Program Description
L739: 
L740: The AppFlowy mentorship program is aimed at creating a hands-on learning
L741: opportunity for new developers who may otherwise lack the opportunity to gain
L742: exposure to real-world software practice and entry to the technical community.
L743: 
L744: Benefits for Mentees:
L745: 
L746: - Mentees gain exposure to real-world software development and entry to the
L747: open-source community.
L748: 
L749: - Mentees become more competitive in the job market by having more meaningful
L750: software development experience.
L751: 
L752: - Mentees have hands-on opportunities to do work related to their professional
L753: interests and to further the pursuit of their interests.
L754: 
L755: - Mentees expand their professional network by getting involved in the community
L756: and meeting other awesome contributors.
L757: 
L758: Benefits for AppFlowy Community:
L759: 
L760: - The mentorship program helps AppFlowy contributors to become AppFlowy core
L761: members and the voice of the community.
L762: 
L763: - The mentorship program helps identify and bring in new developers to our
L764: community.
L765: 
L766: - More source code gets written and used for the benefit of all.
L767: 
L768: We know how satisfied and excited people can be when they are a part of a
L769: community of dedicated developers in open source. We also understand how
L770: overwhelming it can be for newcomers to get started. We would love to offer a
L771: place for developers to get their foot in the door, improve their software
L772: development skills, and for mentorship to thrive.
L773: 
L774: ## Program Schedule
L775: 
L776: Applications are accepted on a rolling basis and applicants are notified of the
L777: decision within 10 days of receipt of a complete proposal. Please use the
L778: suggested proposal template when applying and email your application to
L779: annie@appflowy.io
L780: 
L781: The program requires a commitment of 90 to 180 hours for 6 to 12 weeks. Once you
L782: receive the acceptance letter from us, you are required to create a page about
L783: your project under AppFlowy Docs, which will be marked as your official start
L784: date. A Final evaluation will be conducted at the earlier of the following dates
L785: 1) your choice 2) the end of week 6 or 12.
L786: 
L787: ## Program Structure
L788: 
L789: You will develop both hard and soft skills required for a software engineer in
L790: the real world throughout the program. In addition, you will start playing a role
L791: as an AppFlowy core member and become the voice of our community. The program
L792: will provide you with the opportunity to:
L793: 
L794: - Collect and discuss business requirements cross-functionally
L795: 
L796: - Conduct a tech review to have your mentor and peers review your tech design doc
L797: 
L798: - Give and receive code reviews to/from your peers
L799: 
L800: - Offer help to the community
L801: 
L802: - Know your mentor and peers and participate in online hangouts
L803: 
L804: - Write an article related to your project and get it published to our newsletter
L805: - AppFlowy Binary

L807: ## Getting Started
L808: 
L809: Please use our first-time AppFlowy developer guide to get your AppFlowy
L810: development environment set up and find your first issue. If you have any
L811: trouble, please ask on our community channel.
L812: 
L813: Becoming an AppFlowy contributor is a prerequisite. Newcomers are encouraged to
L814: complete an issue tagged with the “good first issue for devs”. This requires
L815: you to get familiar with our codebase and demonstrates your interest in
L816: contributing to AppFlowy. Don’t worry if you make mistakes in your first
L817: contribution. Instead, please see it as a great opportunity to get involved in
L818: our community, receive feedback, and iterate your work - a flavor of doing a
L819: project with the community.
L820: 
L821: ## Application Instructions
L822: 
L823: Once your PR for an issue tagged with the “good first issue for devs” is
L824: merged, you can start developing a specific project plan. We recommend discussing
L825: your ideas with the community on Discord.
L826: 
L827: Applications are accepted on a rolling basis and applicants are notified of the
L828: decision within 10 days of receipt of a complete proposal. Please use the
L829: suggested proposal template when applying and email your application to
L830: annie@appflowy.io
L831: 
L832: You will need to do thorough research on the AppFlowy codebase, read
L833: documentation, and talk with potential mentors to put together a complete project
L834: proposal. It’s cool to come up with your own project idea as long as your idea
L835: falls under the umbrella of this year’s themes:
L836: 
L837: - Desktop features
L838: 
L839: - CI tools
L840: 
L841: - Tracing performance regressions

L843: Please get in touch with a mentor early on if you want to work on your own idea

L845: applicants to work on one of our ideas. Please see Project Ideas for details.
L846: 
L847: We expect applicants to be excited about gaining real-world software experience
L848: and learning practical skills such as problem-solving and asking well-formed
L849: questions. We also expect applicants to either have experience with the
L850: technologies relevant to their project or have strong general programming
L851: experience. We are happy to accept both student and non-student participants.

L853: Some key criteria for mentees:

L855: - Existing AppFlowy contributor
L856: 
L857: - Likely to become a core community member
L858: 
L859: - Have a passion for AppFlowy
L860: 
L861: - Capable of completing at least 60% of the proposed project with limited
L862: technical guidance

L1036: # Calendar View for AppFlowy Database
L1037: 
L1038: Richard Shiue
L1039: 
L1040: ## Introduction
L1041: 
L1042: AppFlowy's database is an extremely powerful feature that allows users to store
L1043: data in a structured manner. Each database can be customized to contain multiple
L1044: fields, each of a different type, such as text, date and single-selection tags.
L1045: For more information about the terminology used in AppFlowy's database, please
L1046: check out Grid. While the most common way to view the database is in the
L1047: table-view, alternative views can present the data better depending on the use
L1048: case. For example, the kanban board groups entries into columns according to a
L1049: status tag, and is a popular choice for project progress tracking. It also allows
L1050: for new ways to interact with the entries, such as dragging a card from one
L1051: column to another in kanban.
L1052:

L1435: # Favorites
L1436: 
L1437: Mihir Singh
L1438: 
L1439: ## Introduction
L1440: 
L1441: - Managing and organizing vast amounts of data can be a daunting task. Whether
L1442: it's navigating through numerous files and folders or trying to locate specific
L1443: information within a page, the process can often become overwhelming.
L1444: 
L1445: - As users of productivity tools like AppFlowy, we often find ourselves grappling
L1446: with the challenge of efficiently accessing and prioritizing the content that
L1447: matters most to us.
L1448: 
L1449: - A favorite mechanism can alleviate this problem of navigating through a vast
L1450: database by offering users a simple and effective go-to mechanism.
L1451: 
L1452: ## Goal
L1453: 
L1454: Goal of this project is to provide users with efficient mechanism for managing
L1455: and accessing their most important and frequently used content by allowing users
L1456: to mark views as favorites, the feature aims at advanced navigation, organization
L1457: and productivity within the app.
L1458: 
L1459: ## Scope
L1460: 
L1461: 1. Favorite a Page: Users can easily mark a page as a favorite by navigating to
L1462: the desired page and clicking a dedicated button at the top-right corner. This
L1463: action signifies the user's preference for quick access to the selected page.
L1464: 
L1465: 2. Favorites Section: A dedicated Favorites section will be introduced in the
L1466: left sidebar of the AppFlowy interface. Once the user has favorited their first
L1467: page, this section will automatically appear. It provides users with a
L1468: centralized location to find their pinned pages and related subdirectories,
L1469: ensuring easy access to their most important and frequently accessed content.
L1470: 
L1471: 3. Remove from Favorites: Users have the flexibility to unpin or remove a page
L1472: from their Favorites section, allowing them to update their prioritization and
L1473: keep the Favorites section relevant to their current needs and preferences.
L1474: 
L1475: ## Implementation Design
L1476: 
L1477: To implement the favorites feature in AppFlowy, a comprehensive approach
L1478: involving changes in both AppFlowy's rust and flutter components is proposed.
L1479: AppFlowy's persitence logic which was previously part of rust-lib in AppFlowy is
L1480: now separated to a different repository AppFlowy-Collab, current plan is to
L1481: introduce following changes:
L1482: 
L1483: 1. Changes to Existing Persistence Structs (Rust):
L1484: 
L1485: - Each item displayed in the left sidebar will be represented as a `View` struct.
L1486: The concept of an 'App' is deprecated.
L1487: 
L1488: - The `View` struct is defined in the `folder-collab` crate and exposed using the
L1489: `ViewPB` struct.
L1490: 
L1491: - A new variable named `is_favorites` will be introduced in the `View` and
L1492: `ViewPB` structs. This variable will indicate whether a specific view is a
L1493: favorite without the need to iterate through all favorited views.
L1494: 
L1495: 1. Introduction of New Structs (Rust):
L1496: 
L1497: - Two new structs, `FavoritesInfo` and `FavoritesArray`, will be introduced in
L1498: the `collab` module.
L1499: 
L1500: - `FavoritesInfo` will only hold the `view_id` of the favorited view. This will
L1501: allow separate persistence of the favorite views.
L1502: 
L1503: - `FavoritesArray` will utilize `ArrayRefWrapper` and `ViewsMap` as underlying
L1504: constructs to persist all the favorite views.
L1505: 
L1506: 1. Calculation of Favorite Views and Data Transfer (Rust):
L1507: 
L1508: - The handlers in the Rust library ( `rust-lib`) will handle requests from the
L1509: frontend to calculate the views marked as favorites based on user interactions.
L1510: 
L1511: - On every new launch of AppFlowy, a `FolderEvent` named `ReadFavorites` will be
L1512: sent to `rust-lib`. This event will be handled by a `read_favorites_handler`
L1513: function, which will retrieve all the favorite views from persistence, map them
L1514: to `RepeatedViewPB` (a list of `ViewPB`), and return them to the frontend for
L1515: display under the favorites section.
L1516: 
L1517: - When a favorite is toggled for a view, a `FolderEvent` named `ToggleFavorite`
L1518: will be triggered, carrying the `viewId` of the designated view. This event will
L1519: be handled by the `toggle_favorites` function in `rust-lib`.
L1520: 
L1521: - If the view is not currently marked as a favorite, it will be added and
L1522: persisted to the list of favorites.
L1523: 
L1524: - If the view is already marked as a favorite, it will be removed from the list
L1525: of favorites, effectively unfavoriting it.
L1526: 
L1527: - Furthermore, a `ViewPB` will be created and returned to the frontend. This
L1528: `ViewPB` object will represent the updated view and can be appended to the
L1529: visible list of views in the favorites section. This ensures that the UI
L1530: accurately reflects the updated favorite status of the view.
L1531: 
L1532: 1. Notification Handling (Rust):
L1533: 
L1534: - A notification system will be implemented to handle updates to the favorite
L1535: status of views.
L1536: 
L1537: - When the favorite status of a view is updated, a notification named
L1538: `DidUpdateView` under `FolderNotification` will be triggered to update the
L1539: favorite status of the individual view.
L1540: 
L1541: - A `FolderNotification` named `FavoritesUpdated` will be sent every time
L1542: favorite status of a view is updated. This notification will carry a list of the
L1543: updated favorite views, which will be displayed under the favorites section in
L1544: Flutter.
L1545: 
L1546: 1. Integration with UI (Flutter):
L1547: 
L1548: - The Flutter component will incorporate a dedicated bloc and service to handle
L1549: the favorites functionality.
L1550: 
L1551: - This module will be responsible for sending events to `rust-lib` and processing
L1552: the notifications received with those events to appropriately update the views in
L1553: the UI.
L1554: 
L1555: 1. Handling Edge Cases (Flutter):
L1556: 
L1557: - Additional notifications will be handled when a view's data is updated in the
L1558: menu. For example, if a view is renamed, deleted, or its icon is updated, these
L1559: changes will be propagated to the associated view under the favorites section.
L1560:

L1595: # Code Block
L1596: 
L1597: ### Introduction
L1598: 
L1599: Code Block is a feature that allows you to write and display code snippets within
L1600: your notes taken in the AppFlowy Editor. It provides a distinct format for code,
L1601: typically using a monospaced font and syntax highlighting to enhance readability.
L1602: Code blocks are helpful for developers, programmers, and anyone who wants to
L1603: include code snippets or technical instructions within their notes while
L1604: maintaining the visual integrity and readability of the code.
L1605: 
L1606: ### Goal
L1607: 
L1608: The goal of this project is to develop a Code Block in Flutter as a standalone
L1609: package that AppFlowy and other Flutter applications can use. Right now AppFlowy
L1610: uses a Code Block plugin that extends BlockComponentBuilder along with a
L1611: third-party open-source package called highlight.dart for Syntax Highlighting.
L1612: Our goal is to create a standalone package that extends the functionalities of
L1613: the existing solution and serves as a building block for AppFlowy and the Flutter
L1614: Community.
L1615: 
L1616: ### Scope
L1617: 
L1618: The following will be the deliverables by the end of this project:
L1619: 
L1620: - A standalone flutter package for Code Block.
L1621: 
L1622: - Support for the following features in Code Block:
L1623: 
L1624: - Syntax Highlighting
L1625: 
L1626: - Support for Multiple Programming Languages
L1627: 
L1628: - Copy All Code
L1629: 
L1630: - Copy the entire Code Block
L1631: 
L1632: - Line numbering
L1633: 
L1634: - Auto-Indentation
L1635: 
L1636: - Export/import functionality
L1637: 
L1638: ### Existing Solution
L1639: 
L1640: At the moment we have a Code Block plugin which depends on the flutter highlight
L1641: package for syntax highlighting, along with the BlockComponentBuilder API of
L1642: AppFlowy Editor. This current solution only provides the following features we
L1643: want from our Code Block:
L1644: 
L1645: - Syntax highlighting
L1646: 
L1647: - Support for multiple programming languages
L1648: 
L1649: We are looking to extract our Code Block plugin code and create a separate
L1650: package for it. We aim to extend its functionalities to support all the features
L1651: we want in our Code Block solution.
L1652: 
L1653: ### Proposed Solution Design
L1654: 
L1655: This is what we expect from our implementation. We want the line numbering to
L1656: appear in the left edge of our codeblock. Our actions relating to the CodeBlock

L1759: # Outlines
L1760: 
L1761: Aman Negi
L1762: 
L1763: ### Introduction
L1764: 
L1765: AppFlowy is a versatile tool with a wide range of use cases. As a result,
L1766: documents created in AppFlowy can vary significantly in length and complexity. To
L1767: address this, it would be beneficial to develop an Outline Plugin that would
L1768: display all of the headings in a document at the beginning, making it easier for
L1769: users to scan and navigate the document.
L1770: 
L1771: ### Goals
L1772: 
L1773: The goals of the AppFlowy Outline Plugin are to:
L1774: 
L1775: - Provide a quick and easy way to navigate through long and complex documents
L1776: 
L1777: - Help users to find specific information in a document more quickly
L1778: 
L1779: - Provide a visual overview of the document's structure
L1780: 
L1781: - Help users to understand the document's content
L1782: 
L1783: ### Scope
L1784: 
L1785: The AppFlowy Outline Plugin will add the following new actions to the AppFlowy
L1786: application:
L1787: 
L1788: - Users will be able to add an outline to a document using the slash ( `/`) menu.
L1789: 
L1790: - The content of the outline will be automatically generated based on the
L1791: document.
L1792: 
L1793: - Clicking on the content of the outline will take users directly to the
L1794: corresponding heading.
L1795: 
L1796: - In the outline different levels of headings will be indented differently. For
L1797: example, H1 will have no indentation, while H2 will be indented once, and so on.
L1798: 
L1799: - Only H1, H2, and H3 headings will be shown in the outline. Other elements will
L1800: not be displayed or represented.
L1801: 
L1802: ### Implementation
L1803: 
L1804: To keep the encapsulate the Outline feature, we created it as an `editor_plugin`
L1805: and simply plugged it into the editor.

L1810:

L1813: # Importers
L1814: 
L1815: Mukund Tandon
L1816: 
L1817: ### Introduction
L1818: 
L1819: AppFlowy is a powerful knowledge management tool that empowers users to organize
L1820: their work, take notes, ideate and plan effectively. To enhance the onboarding
L1821: experience and facilitate a seamless transition for new users, Importers project
L1822: will allow users to migrate their existing data from Third-party applications(eg
L1823: -Notion) to AppFlowy. This will contain a number of features which would help in
L1824: importing data. This aims to simplify the migration process and enable users to
L1825: continue working with their valuable content within AppFlowy.
L1826: 
L1827: ### Goals
L1828: 
L1829: The goal of this project is to make it easy for AppFlowy users to migrate their
L1830: data from Third-party applications like Notion. First I would be focusing on
L1831: Notion-
L1832: 
L1833: - \[ \] Convert Notion document page to AppFlowy document page
L1834: 
L1835: - Allow notion user to easily import a complete page to AppFlowy .When the user
L1836: clicks on export on Notion page it gives us a zip file which user can import to
L1837: AppFlowy . This will import the page along with the subpages of that pages and
L1838: the assets of that page.
L1839: 
L1840: - Also fix the current implementation of importing using markdown to support all
L1841: elements which are supported in AppFlowy but are missing in import example
L1842: codeblocks, images.
L1843: 
L1844: - Enable appflowy-editor users to effortlessly convert their custom Markdown
L1845: syntax into custom nodes using the `markdownToDocument` function, with the
L1846: assistance of custom parsers. With custom parsers, users can specify how they
L1847: want a particular Markdown syntax to be transformed into a specific node.
L1848: 
L1849: - Importing a large file may take a significant amount of time. If the app
L1850: crashes during the import process, it can result in an incomplete import. If the
L1851: user initiates another import, it may lead to the creation of duplicate files, as
L1852: some files have already been imported before and are being imported again. Thus
L1853: we have to handle this edge case. Also we want to perform this importing in
L1854: background, so the user can continue to work while the importing is happening.
L1855: 
L1856: - Add a option on Import panel to import calendar from notion
L1857: 
L1858: - \[ \] Convert Notion calendar to AppFlowy calendar
L1859: 
L1860: - Rust -> Support populating the Calendar page from the imported folder which
L1861: contains a CSV file and a folder containing markdown file of notes for each date.
L1862: 
L1863: - Flutter -> Add a option on Import panel to import calendar from notion
L1864: 
L1865: - \[ \] Convert Notion board to AppFlowy Board
L1866: 
L1867: - Rust -> Populating the board with the data from the CSV file which contains
L1868: information regarding the column under which each card should be placed on the
L1869: board. Then there is a folder containing the contents of each card. So we need to
L1870: populate the cards with their respective contents.
L1871: 
L1872: - Flutter -> Add an option on Import panel to import board from notion
L1873: 
L1874: - \[ \] Convert Notion Database to AppFlowy Grid
L1875: 
L1876: - Rust -> AppFlowy currently supports importing CSV , So we can import the grid
L1877: contents from Notion but in Notion each row is a page and can contain more
L1878: information than that given in the grid so have to also import those pages. When
L1879: we export the Notion Database we get a folder containing a CSV file and and
L1880: number of markdown files .We can use the CSV file to populate AppFlowy grid and
L1881: can import the each page from the markdown files from the folder
L1882: 
L1883: - Flutter -> Add a option on Import panel to import Database from notion.
L1884: 
L1885: - \[ \] Option to upload the contents of complete workspace from notion to
L1886: AppFlowy
L1887: 
L1888: - Rust -> When we export our workspace we get a folder which contains many sub
L1889: folders having information regarding each page. So we need to populate all the
L1890: pages and subpages in the correct manner including all databases calendars and
L1891: boards
L1892: 
L1893: - Flutter -> Add a option on Import panel to import workspace from notion.
L1894: 
L1895: ### Scope
L1896: 
L1897: On completion of this -
L1898: 
L1899: - There will be an option in the Import panel that says "Import from Notion."
L1900: Upon clicking on it, users will be able to select what they want to import, such
L1901: as boards, grids, calendars, pages, or the entire workspace.

L1903: - Users will be able to import a single page from Notion and all contents from
L1904: that page which are supported in AppFlowy will get imported

L1906: - Users will be able to import their calendars from Notion
L1907: 
L1908: - Users will be able to import their board from Notion
L1909: 
L1910: - Users will be able to import their database from Notion including the subpages.
L1911: 
L1912: - Users will be to import their complete workspace from Notion. There would be an
L1913: option to select the folder(provided by Notion) which contains all the exported
L1914: contents, and all the contents(supported by AppFlowy) from that folder will be
L1915: imported into AppFlowy with all the pages and subpages in correct manner
L1916: including all databases calendars and boards

L1918: ## Implementation Details
L1919: 
L1920: ### Importing Page from Notion-
L1921: 
L1922: #### What does a page look like when exported from Notion-
L1923: 
L1924: We get a zip file containing the the main page markdown and a folder containing
L1925: assets of the main page and also markdown files of subpages of the main page and
L1926: folders containing the assets of the subpages and the sub-sub pages markdown
L1927: files and so on.
L1928: 
L1929: #### How our main page markdown file look
L1930: 
L1931: We can see on line 5,6 we have two images inside the round brackets is the path
L1932: where images are located and on line 19,21,23 are sub-pages
L1933: 
L1934: #### Markdown file of sub-page
L1935: 
L1936: Here we have to look at the image path it starts with AppFlowy Subpage 1 instead
L1937: of instead of AppFlowy Test which is the parent folder. This is because it’s
L1938: asset lies in AppFlowy Sub 1 folder which is at the same level where the subpage
L1939: markdown file is . This fact will be used late while importing.
L1940: 
L1941: * * *
L1942: 
L1943: #### How is the Importing working
L1944: 
L1945: - First we iterate through the unzipped files list and store all files and assets
L1946: in there respective level in the `levels` list
L1947: 
L1948: - Next step will be importing all the pages present starting from the last
L1949: level.we are importing from the last level to handle the case of subpages . For
L1950: parent page to show `MentionBlock` of the subpage it requires the SubPage viewID
L1951: which can only be generated once it is imported so we import the lowest level sub
L1952: page first and then go up storing each page viewID in a map (nameToID) which has
L1953: key as the page name and value as the page viewID.
L1954: 
L1955: - Next once we have all page imported we would move them under their respective
L1956: parent
L1957: 
L1958: This class contains details of each page to be imported and the parent of that
L1959: page which will be used for moving the page under correct parent in later steps
L1960: 
L1961: This class contains details of each level of the files. Like For example the main
L1962: page will be level one , if it has a subpage it will be level 2 and if that
L1963: subpage will have another subpage that would belong to level 3
L1964: 
L1965: #### When we are importing a markdown page how are we dealing with images
L1966: 
L1967: - To deal with images we take all contents of a markdown file and pass it through
L1968: `_preProcessMarkdownFile` function which returns us a string which is the
L1969: contents of the markdown file but with changes. The changes this function
L1970: performs are related to images . It will iterate through each line and if it
L1971: finds something like `![name](path)` this is how a image is represented in
L1972: markdown . When we get this line is detected we get the path from this this path
L1973: is actually the file name of image from the above list of unzip images so with
L1974: the help of path we will get the image file and save it locally and change the
L1975: current path to the path where the image is saved locally
L1976: 
L1977: - Now the problem we can see here is as discussed before the path name in a sub
L1978: page starts with AppFlowy Sub page instead of Appflowy test which is the root .
L1979: In the above list also you can see that all the file name are starting from
L1980: AppFlowy Test so if we directly pass this list to `_preProcessMarkdownFile` it
L1981: wont be able find the image file.So this issue was solve by only passing the
L1982: assets of a particular level to the \_preProcessMarkdownFile function instead of
L1983: all the assets and also during the process of adding files/assets in the levels
L1984: list if a file is not added in the particular level then the first part(parent)
L1985: from it name would be removed
L1986: 
L1987: #### How does Subpages are handled while importing a page ?
L1988: 
L1989: We are imported from level 3 to level 1. This is done because to handle the
L1990: subpages . We use `markdownToDocument` function of appflowy-editor package to
L1991: chick we pass the markdown contents of our page and it return us a Document. We
L1992: also pass a custom-parser to this function which handles our subpage. Whenever it
L1993: detects a subpage it replace the part with a `MentionBlock`(It contains the
L1994: pageID of the page that is being Mentioned) . This is reason we are importing the
L1995: lower level page first . We will import them and store their viewID in a map
L1996: where the key is pageName and value is the pageID. When above level are being
L1997: imported and there contents are passed through `_preProcessMarkdownFile` function
L1998: this map(nameToId) is also passed in the function , whenever it finds a subpage
L1999: which looks like name to `{{AppFlowy-Subpage}}{$subpageName}{$subPageID}` , this
L2000: pattern is used in custom parser to detect the subpage part and convert it to
L2001: mention block. We have stored the pageIds with name as key so we can easily get
L2002: the pageID of subpage by using name from name .

L2349: # Templates
L2350: 
L2351: Aman Negi
L2352: 
L2353: ## Introduction
L2354: 
L2355: AppFlowy is a powerful Open-Source Notion alternative, and we are rapidly
L2356: improving the application to provide a seamless experience. As of writing this
L2357: doc, we support nested documents, grids, boards, calendars, and referenced
L2358: documents/grids. Using these tits and bits you can combine and create your own
L2359: perfect workspace. While having all these features is excellent, creating your
L2360: ideal workplace from scratch every time can be cumbersome.
L2361: 
L2362: ## Goal
L2363: 
L2364: The goal of this project is to provide a template feature, where users can create
L2365: templates from a `Zip` File, and can also export a template. Users can use a
L2366: template created by the community or reuse their own templates. Later, we plan to
L2367: have a Template Marketplace where users can share their templates with others.
L2368: However, that would be out of the scope of this project and a different feature
L2369: altogether.
L2370: 
L2371: ## Scope
L2372: 
L2373: By the completion of this project, the user will be able to:
L2374: 
L2375: - \[x\] Export existing pages as templates in ZIP format.
L2376: 
L2377: - \[x\] Import templates by selecting the ZIP file, which will recreate the
L2378: original structure with its content.
L2379: 
L2380: - \[x\] Import/Export nested pages and databases.
L2381: 
L2382: - \[ \] Maintain references between referenced databases and Linked Pages while
L2383: importing/exporting.
L2384: 
L2385: - \[ \] Support exporting assets, while exporting a document.
L2386: 
L2387: ## Implementation Design
L2388: 
L2389: To implement the template feature, we came ahead with a simple but efficient
L2390: solution. Further, we will discuss the implementation of the import and export
L2391: templates separately.
L2392: 
L2393: ### Export Template:
L2394: 
L2395: In AppFlowy, we previously provided the following features for exporting:
L2396: 
L2397: - Export a document as `.json` or `.md` file.
L2398: 
L2399: - Export a database as `.csv` file.
L2400: 
L2401: In the export template feature, we wanted to provide the user with the capability
L2402: of exporting multiple pages and documents as a whole package. Another critical
L2403: decision was to decide how to save the data regarding the structure of the pages,
L2404: which could be then used as a reference to import the pages in the same
L2405: structure.
L2406: 
L2407: To store the document structure and configuration, we decided to generate a
L2408: `config.json` file during exporting that would contain all the details about the
L2409: template. During, importing a template the same config file would be used to
L2410: understand the structure of the template.
L2411: 
L2412: Example of `config.json `
L2413: 
L2414: - To generate the config file we created a `ConfigService` which does all the
L2415: heavy lifting i.e. generating `config.json` using the current `ViewPB`.
L2416: 
L2417: - Once, the config file is generated we then use `TemplateService` to simply
L2418: export all the pages, databases, and the config file.
L2419: 
L2420: > By default the exported files are stored in `documents/template/` folder.
L2421: 
L2422: The export process is completed at this point and the exports can be Zipped into
L2423: a single `.zip` file which is then ready to be imported!
L2424: 
L2425: Flow of export template
L2426: 
L2427: ### Import Template:
L2428: 
L2429: Importing documents and databases was previously supported in AppFlowy, however,
L2430: under this feature, we would support importing a complete structure of documents
L2431: and databases. Previously we created a `config.json` file while exporting, we
L2432: would now use it for importing the template.
L2433: 
L2434: - Click on the add button and select the template option as shown.
L2435: 
L2436: Select the template option
L2437: 
L2438: - Now the file picker will be opened and you can now select the `tempate.zip`
L2439: generated in the export section. Once you select the template ZIP it will be
L2440: added to your editor.
L2441: 
L2442: Flow of importing a template

L2687: ## Are you an AppFlowy enthusiast? Help other AppFlowy users and builders, get

L2689: 
L2690: Whether you’re an AppFlowy power user, a software development expert, or just a
L2691: student starting to get into open source, there is knowledge you can share that
L2692: will benefit the entire AppFlowy community.

L2697: 
L2698: - Discussions about specific use cases

L2702: You will be paid for articles published on AppFlowy Binary and pages posted to

L2704: created.

L2707: profile of your choosing.

L2710: record to help with style, grammar, and content. Please email your portfolio to
L2711: career@appflowy.io

L2713: ## How does it work?
L2714: 
L2715: #### Post to Discord About Your Topic
L2716: 
L2717: First, join our Discord channel and create a post. Your post should include the
L2718: topic you want to cover and an outline. The topic can be your own or select an
L2719: existing GitHub issue tagged with “ write-for-appflowy".
L2720: 
L2721: #### Wait for Approval on the Topic
L2722: 
L2723: Once you create a post, the AppFlowy team will review it. It may take a few days
L2724: or weeks for us to review.
L2725: 
L2726: If we shortlist your topic, we will work with you to refine the scope and outline
L2727: of the article to ensure the result is informative and engaging.
L2728: 
L2729: We will then create a GitHub issue for the topic and assign the issue to you.
L2730: 
L2731: #### Get Feedback
L2732: 
L2733: After you finish the first draft, you are encouraged to get feedback from the
L2734: AppFlowy team and a few community members who are your article’s target
L2735: audience.
L2736: 
L2737: You should be aware that not every submitted article will be published.
L2738: 
L2739: #### Publication of Your Article
L2740: 
L2741: Once your article is reviewed and published on our blog, you can submit your
L2742: invoice to get paid via Deel.
L2743: 
L2744: But that’s not all — we’ll also promote your work on our social media
L2745: channels, providing greater exposure for your work.
L2746: 
L2747: #### Ongoing Support
L2748: 
L2749: Ongoing support is required. You should promptly respond to queries about your
L2750: published work. How-to guides should remain up-to-date.
L2751: 
L2752: We expect that you will provide support for at least 30 days after your article
L2753: is published. Future engagements will be contingent on how well existing articles
L2754: are supported.
L2755: 
L2756: We may archive your how-to guides if it’s not up-to-date given that our product
L2757: is still under rapid development and may evolve pretty quickly.

L3222: # \[Draft\] How to add a new property to appflowy database
L3223: 
L3224: One of the things you can do in Appflowy is work with structured data (it's
L3225: called Appflowy databases) and view them in different layouts, such as Table,
L3226: Board, Calendar.
L3227: 
L3228: In this article, I will take a look at how the back-end part of Appflowy
L3229: databases works overall and share a more detailed guide on how to create a new
L3230: property type.
L3231: 
L3232: ## Flowy-database
L3233: 
L3234: Flowy-database is a rust crate mainly responsible for the abstractions behind
L3235: Appflowy databases, CRUD actions on data, storing, filtering and etc. Let's take
L3236: a look at the code structure and dive in (the picture is only the directories you
L3237: can take a more detailed look here).
L3238: 
L3239: ### Entities
L3240: 
L3241: Basic abstractions that Flowy-database uses to model the data and work with them
L3242: behind the scene. I will describe some of them a bit.
L3243: 
L3244: #### Cell
L3245: 
L3246: Most basic abstraction that encapsulates the raw data and determines its row and
L3247: column.
L3248: 
L3249: #### Row
L3250: 
L3251: Multiple cells packaged together. In table view, it's the table row and in board
L3252: view each card represents a row.
L3253: 
L3254: #### Field
L3255: 
L3256: Think of it as sort of table columns. Closely related to Property, It creates a
L3257: link between different cells and determines their type. Each field has a type
L3258: (not unique) for example Number, Text, Email, Date, etc. Will say more about
L3259: fields on "How to add new property type" section.
L3260: 
L3261: #### Sort
L3262: 
L3263: For sorting rows based on a specific field and condition, which will be based on
L3264: one of the row's cells. This is mostly useful in Table layout.
L3265: 
L3266: #### Filter
L3267: 
L3268: To filter out and show only some rows based on a condition you can use filters.
L3269: Filter has a general part ( `FilterPB`), for example which field is this filter
L3270: for and a custom part which is different based on mostly the field type. So for
L3271: the Number field type, we can have filter which specifies the cell related to the
L3272: Number field should be greater than the user-specified number. And for a Checkbox
L3273: field type, we can have a filter that the cell should be checked.
L3274: 
L3275: Where to start with adding new filter condition
L3276: 
L3277: If you want to add new filter condition for your desired field type in Appflowy.
L3278: First you have to find the specific field type filter entity or create it if
L3279: doesn't exist. Second, add your filter condition name in the field type
L3280: conditions enum. Third in services->field->type\_option->field\_type, you have to
L3281: determine how applying that filter condition should take effect. See the
L3282: `apply_filter` method for each type option.
L3283: 
L3284: #### Group
L3285: 
L3286: This is for grouping multiple rows by a common field. This is used mostly in
L3287: Board layout. For example, grouping your tasks (rows) by their priority which
L3288: priority here is a field with single select type.
L3289: 
L3290: Where to start with adding a new group by
L3291: 
L3292: For enabling group by a specific field you should add its controller in
L3293: services->group->controller\_impls. The controller has to implement
L3294: `GroupCustomize` trait.
L3295: 
L3296: ### Events
L3297: 
L3298: There are two types of events in Flowy-database internal and external. Here I'm
L3299: going to describe external events. This is the way Appflowy front-ends and
L3300: back-end talk to each other. In the event\_map file, you can see the handler that
L3301: each event will trigger. The handler will also usually fetch `DatabaseEditor`
L3302: service and use it to do the job.
L3303: 
L3304: ### Services
L3305: 
L3306: Services are where the core of the logic exists and it's the way to manipulate
L3307: data. You can create, delete, update data (rows, cells, properties, ...) via
L3308: services.
L3309: 
L3310: You can see more documentation on Appflowy databases here.
L3311: 
L3312: ## How to add new property type
L3313: 
L3314: Now with some knowledge that how Flowy-database is structured, we can take a look
L3315: at a practical example. Let's first see what is property and then go further.
L3316: 
L3317: ### Property
L3318: 
L3319: You can create as many properties as you want for your database in Appflowy.
L3320: Property is showed differently regarding the view of your database, In table view
L3321: (layout) it's column of your table (each column is a separate property).
L3322: 
L3323: As I said properties are tightly related to Field entity abstraction. So on
L3324: creating new property, you create a new `Field` in Flowy-database. Each `Field`
L3325: data structure has `name` and `field_type`. The name is what you see as the
L3326: property name and the type is something you select from available field types
L3327: (e.g Number, Text, Checkbox, Select, etc).
L3328: 
L3329: If you want to introduce a new property type you have to add a new field type (
L3330: `FieldType`) in Flowy-database. Here comes the "type option" data structure.
L3331: 
L3332: #### Type Option
L3333: 
L3334: `field_type` on `Field` is an enum type named `FieldType` it doesn't hold any
L3335: data. Each `FieldType` is mapped to a specific type option which has to implement
L3336: the `TypeOption` trait. This is done in type option service. So for example for a
L3337: Checkbox field type, we have `CheckboxTypeOption` which includes a simple
L3338: `is_selected` property with bool type.
L3339: 
L3340: Note that every field type should get linked to a type option but it's not
L3341: necessarily a one-to-one relation, it can be many-to-one. As you will see
L3342: multiple field types can link to the same type option.
L3343: 
L3344: #### Filter
L3345: 
L3346: If you want to enable filtering for your field type you also have to add a filter
L3347: entity for it (in entities->filter\_entities). See the samples in source code.
L3348: 
L3349: Now let's create a new property step by step.
L3350: 
L3351: ### Let's create new property "Created At" and "Updated At"
L3352: 
L3353: I'm writing this closely after my merge request on adding CreatedAt and UpdatedAt
L3354: property type has got merged. So when you are reading this Appflowy has these two
L3355: types as a property type. But here I will assume they are not implemented yet,
L3356: and we will go through implementing them step by step, I won't go through detail
L3357: every specifics but I will elaborate the parts which I think are essential.
L3358: 
L3359: Note that Appflowy code is changing constantly so the specific names and codes
L3360: that I mention here may change in time and you may see differences when you are
L3361: reading this, but the overall process of adding new property type will probably
L3362: be more stable.
L3363: 
L3364: #### What do we want?
L3365: 
L3366: For CreatedAt we want a property type which gets set on creating new row. So it
L3367: will record the time when the row is created.
L3368: 
L3369: UpdatedAt is similar in some ways. With this property type we want to record last
L3370: time the row has been modified. So it should get set each time the row is
L3371: modified.
L3372: 
L3373: #### Adding the new field type
L3374: 
L3375: For every property type it is a must to create new field type on `FieldType`
L3376: enum. So we have to add two new field type CreatedAt and UpdatedAt. Now that I'm
L3377: writing this beside these two that we are adding, there are 8 field types in
L3378: Flowy-database. Among them Date field type which is close to our desired field
L3379: types CreatedAt and UpdatedAt.
L3380: 
L3381: #### Deciding to introduce new type option or not
L3382: 
L3383: After adding two new field types we should decide about type option. As I said
L3384: before we have Date field type which has date type option. If you think through
L3385: you may agree with me that CreatedAt and UpdatedAt are the same as Date regarding
L3386: the data they contain.
L3387: 
L3388: There is a timestamp which records the date (it's not in date type option but in
L3389: date cell data), time format, date format and timezone for customizing the
L3390: display. All four are also applicable to CreatedAt and UpdatedAt. The difference
L3391: is the way the data gets set which is not related to the type option.
L3392: 
L3393: So we will use date type option for our new field types. With some tweaks this is
L3394: possible (adding `field_type` on the date type option), you can see them in the
L3395: merge request.
L3396: 
L3397: #### Connecting field types to type option
L3398: 
L3399: We decided to use date type option for our new field types. Still we should
L3400: connect date type option to these new field types. This is done in:
L3401: 
L3402: 1. type option service in `type_option_data_from_pb_or_default` function to
L3403: create date type option from raw data and in `type_option_to_pb` function which
L3404: date type option to raw data.
L3405: 
L3406: 2. Again the type option service in `default_type_option_data_from_type` function
L3407: for creating date type option with default values.
L3408: 
L3409: 3. In `get_type_option_cell_data_handler` and `get_type_option_transform_handler`
L3410: function for getting `TypeOptionCellDataHandler` and
L3411: `TypeOptionTransformHandler`. Also for filters it's done in implementing from
L3412: `Filter` to `FilterPB`.
L3413: 
L3414: #### Hooking into events and modifying services
L3415: 
L3416: Now that we are done with field type, type option we should implement what makes
L3417: CreatedAt and UpdatedAt distinguish from Date field type, and that is how they
L3418: get filled.
L3419: 
L3420: We want to set each cell with CreatedAt and UpdatedAt field type when a new row
L3421: is created and keep updating the cell with UpdatedAt field type whenever the row
L3422: gets modified.
L3423: 
L3424: There is a `CreateRow` database event which is connected to `create_row_handler`
L3425: there we see that cells are created by `CellBuilder::with_cells` method. In the
L3426: first part row cells are filled based on data received. The data is parsed based
L3427: on cell field type. Here we can decide to enable setting cells with UpdatedAt and
L3428: CreatedAt field type manually or not (for example allowing user to change cell
L3429: with CreatedAt field type).
L3430: 
L3431: After the first part, we should change the method so it checks if the row has
L3432: cells with UpdatedAt or CreatedAt field types and set them to the current
L3433: timestamp. So every time a row is created these cells will get filled
L3434: automatically. This is enough for CreatedAt field type. But for UpdatedAt we need
L3435: to do more.
L3436: 
L3437: The cells with UpdatedAt field type should get updated whenever any other cell of
L3438: the row is modified. If we look at the event map there is an `UpdateCell`
L3439: database event connected to `update_cell_handler`, This is the lead we should
L3440: follow. We can see `update_cell_handler` calls `update_cell_with_changeset`
L3441: method of `DatabaseEditor` which also at the end calls `update_cell`. What we
L3442: want to implement here is to update UpdatedAt cells and set them to the current
L3443: timestamp after the requested cell is updated.
L3444: 
L3445: #### Enabling the new property types in front-end
L3446: 
L3447: This is it.
L3448: 
L3449: 1. We added the new field type
L3450: 
L3451: 2. Made connections from new field types to the date type option
L3452: 
L3453: 3. We modified the necessary services to change the cells with our new field type
L3454: as we desire.
L3455: 
L3456: Now for seeing our new property type in action. We have to build Flowy-database
L3457: again. Choose one of Appflowy front-ends and make some changes (which are mostly
L3458: just mentioning the field type enum). And at last build the front-end.
L3459: 
L3460: ## Contribute to Appflowy by implementing new property types
L3461: 
L3462: You can start contributing to Appflowy by implementing new property types. Look
L3463: at what we currently have. Create an issue for your desired missing property type
L3464: and start implementing it after it's accepted.

L3927: # Architecture
L3928: 
L3929: Skeleton architecture provides a foundational structure for a software system
L3930: without specifying the full details. It serves as a high-level framework,
L3931: defining the essential components and their relationships, allowing developers to
L3932: build upon it and flesh out the system's functionality as needed. It's a flexible
L3933: and adaptable starting point for software development.
L3934: 
L3935: Why the Skeleton Architecture?
L3936: 
L3937: Skeleton architecture serves as a crucial starting point for our software
L3938: development projects.
L3939: 
L3940: Here's why we choose to implement it:
L3941: 
L3942: 1. Efficiency: Skeleton architecture jumpstarts development, reducing setup time
L3943: and accelerating the initial stages of the project.
L3944: 
L3945: 2. Adaptability: It provides a flexible foundation that can easily evolve to meet
L3946: changing project requirements and new features.
L3947: 
L3948: 3. Reliability: Defining the basic structure helps avoid architectural
L3949: oversights, leading to a more dependable system.
L3950: 
L3951: 4. Scalability: As the project grows, the skeleton architecture accommodates the
L3952: addition of more detailed components and functionality.
L3953: 
L3954: 5. Consistency: It fosters code uniformity and design patterns across the
L3955: project, improving readability and maintainability.
L3956: 
L3957: 6. Cost-Effectiveness: Using skeleton architecture saves resources by
L3958: streamlining the development process.
L3959: 
L3960: 7. Communication: It facilitates clear communication and project visualization,
L3961: helping all stakeholders understand the project's foundational structure.
L3962: 
L3963: There are other reasons as well, but these are some of the more prominent ones as
L3964: to why Skeleton Architecture could be preferred.

L4051: and registration process, making it easy for new users to join while ensuring
L4052: platform security and confidentiality of user data.
L4053: 
L4054: - Online Mailbox and Document Management: The platform provides robust online
L4055: document management capabilities. Users can access and edit their documents on
L4056: any device and manage emails through an integrated mailbox, making communication
L4057: and file management more efficient.

L4059: ## Design Philosophy
L4060: 
L4061: In this project, we implement a three-tier architecture: Data Fetching Layer,
L4062: Data Processing Layer, and Data Rendering Layer. This structured approach is
L4063: designed to enhance our development efficiency and simplify problem-solving by
L4064: focusing on key principles:
L4065: 
L4066: 1. Simplicity is Efficiency : We prioritize straightforward solutions to support
L4067: rapid development and facilitate easier understanding, which helps in maintaining
L4068: a low error rate and reducing complexity.
L4069: 
L4070: 2. Reducing Heavy Dependencies : Our architecture promotes high cohesion and low
L4071: coupling through a modular design where each layer handles specific functions
L4072: independently. This structure minimizes inter-layer dependencies, enhancing
L4073: flexibility and maintainability.
L4074: 
L4075: 3. Functional Programming Principles : By applying functional programming
L4076: techniques, we emphasize immutable data structures and pure functions. This
L4077: approach not only simplifies data handling and state management but also makes
L4078: the code more predictable and easier to test.
L4079: 
L4080: 4. Simplifying Complex Problems : We break down complex issues into smaller,
L4081: manageable parts by clearly defining layer responsibilities. This method ensures
L4082: that developers are not bogged down by the intricacies of the code, fostering a
L4083: more enjoyable and effective problem-solving environment.
L4084: 
L4085: Our goal with this architecture is to create a development environment that not
L4086: only meets the current technical demands but also remains manageable and
L4087: enjoyable for our team. By adhering to these principles, we aim to produce a
L4088: robust system with fewer bugs and higher overall productivity.
L4089: 
L4090: ## ️ Technology Stack
L4091: 
L4092: - React.js: A JavaScript library for building user interfaces, React.js is the

L4094: for creating interactive and dynamic web applications.
L4095:

L4098: work on the same document simultaneously, making it ideal for team projects and
L4099: shared documents.
L4100:

L4105: ## Module Composition
L4106: 
L4107: AppFlowy Web is architected around three key modules, ensuring efficient data
L4108: handling and flexible frontend rendering:
L4109: 
L4110: 1. Data Fetching: Responsible for obtaining data from backend APIs or other
L4111: external data sources. This layer focuses on the initial reception of data,
L4112: including user inputs and external API calls.
L4113: 
L4114: 2. Data Processing: Handles necessary data manipulation and state management
L4115: before rendering. This layer leverages Yjs to manage data states, ensuring
L4116: synchronization and real-time updates in multi-user scenarios.
L4117: 
L4118: 3. Data Rendering: Builds and renders the final user interface. Utilizing React,
L4119: this module constructs responsive UIs that dynamically update based on user
L4120: interactions and data changes.
L4121: 
L4122: These modules work together to facilitate a smooth data flow from acquisition to
L4123: presentation, optimizing user experience and system responsiveness.
L4124: 
L4125: ### Data Fetching
L4126: 
L4127: In AppFlowy Web, the Data Fetching module employs a WebAssembly (WASM) library
L4128: provided by AppFlowy, instead of traditional HTTP methods. This choice is based
L4129: on practical reasons:
L4130: 
L4131: 1. Code Reusability: Using the same WASM library as the desktop client allows for
L4132: a consistent and reusable codebase across platforms. This uniformity aids in
L4133: maintaining and updating the software more efficiently.
L4134: 
L4135: 2. Technical Exploration: Choosing WASM is part of an effort to learn and
L4136: integrate newer technologies within the project. This provides the development
L4137: team with experience in newer web development practices.
L4138: 
L4139: The adoption of WASM, despite its potential to increase bundle sizes, reflects an
L4140: interest in exploring how emerging technologies can be fitted into and benefit
L4141: the project.
L4142: 
L4143: ### Data Processing
L4144: 
L4145: The Data Processing module in AppFlowy Web links the data fetching and rendering
L4146: stages, focusing on preparing data for use:
L4147: 
L4148: 1. Service Layer Connection: Connects to the fetching module and implements
L4149: caching strategies to speed up data availability for rendering. The service
L4150: provides access to the original data (YDoc) for the rendering layer.
L4151: 
L4152: 1. Data Manipulation Methods: Raw data obtained from the service is not
L4153: immediately suitable for rendering and requires processing:
L4154: 
L4155: - Publish Provider: Manages publishing-related data operations, providing
L4156: interfaces and hooks for data access.
L4157: 
L4158: - Document Transfer: Handles the conversion between Slate data and Yjs data,
L4159: manages update listeners, and performs granular updates necessary for document
L4160: synchronization.
L4161: 
L4162: - Database Operations: Monitors YDoc updates to facilitate data querying,
L4163: sorting, grouping, and fetching specific rows and columns. This layer controls
L4164: component updates based on the data fetched from various interfaces.
L4165: 
L4166: This module ensures data is correctly processed and ready for rendering,
L4167: supporting the application's operational flow.
L4168: 
L4169: ### Data Rendering
L4170: 
L4171: The Data Rendering module in AppFlowy Web is primarily responsible for rendering
L4172: components within the application. This module utilizes the React framework to
L4173: manage and update the user interface based on data changes:
L4174: 
L4175: 1. Integration with Data Processing: Although data handling is often separated
L4176: for maintenance purposes, data processing and rendering are inherently linked.
L4177: This separation helps in maintaining clarity and manageability in the codebase
L4178: but recognizes that some level of data processing is necessary directly at the
L4179: rendering stage.
L4180: 
L4181: 2. React Framework: Components are rendered using React, which relies on
L4182: data-driven updates through props and state management. React's context mechanism
L4183: is also employed to pass down data and provide accessibility across different
L4184: components without prop-drilling.
L4185: 
L4186: This approach ensures that the application remains responsive and efficient,
L4187: updating only the necessary parts of the user interface when data changes occur.

L4321: ## Grid
L4322: 
L4323: At its core, a Grid type is a simple representation of items placed in columns
L4324: and rows. It is not a spreadsheet.
L4325: 
L4326: Another name for a column is Field. A column's configuration is defined in the
L4327: Field class. It is important to note though that although a grid has the concept
L4328: of columns, there are no actual Column classes.
L4329: 
L4330: A user can add a Row, and then define the data in each of the cells created for
L4331: the Grid's Fields in that row.

L4333: ## Cache

L4335: When you open a grid, a `GridBloc` will be initialized. There are four cache
L4336: classes, as shown in the diagram above.

L4338: 1. `GridRowCache `

L4340: - Caches the `grid`'s `Row ` s in memory.
L4341: 
L4342: - A `Row` contains many `Cells, each` Cell `will be cached in the `

L4347: 1. `GridCellCache `

L4353: ## Field
L4354: 
L4355: ### Field
L4356: 
L4357: A `Field` represents a column's configuration. It will contain the column's name,
L4358: id, width, type (as defined in FieldType), etc.
L4359: 
L4360: ### FieldType
L4361: 
L4362: A `Field` has a `FieldType`. The `FieldType` defines the kind of data contained
L4363: in a column. For example, a column may contain dates, numbers, text, multi-select
L4364: list, etc.
L4365: 
L4366: Certain field types have user-defined options such as color, date format, number
L4367: format, or a list of values for a multi-select list. These options are defined
L4368: within a specialization of the `FieldTypeOption` class.
L4369: 
L4370: Each field has its `TypeOptionBuilder` in the backend that is used to parse the
L4371: bytes into corresponding FieldTypeOption.
L4372: 
L4373: ### FieldEditor
L4374: 
L4375: FieldEditor
L4376: 
L4377: A `FieldEditor` is a widget that is used to edit the field's shared properties.
L4378: Such as the name of the field, etc. It uses the `FieldTypeOptionEditor` to
L4379: customize the UI for each field.
L4380: 
L4381: FieldEditorBloc
L4382: 
L4383: `FieldEditorBloc` uses a `TypeOptionDataController` to listen for changes to a
L4384: `Field` or perform a rename operation. It will notify the widget to rebuild if
L4385: its state has changed.
L4386: 
L4387: TypeOptionDataController
L4388: 
L4389: Defines how to update a `Field`'s properties. Such as the name, the field, and
L4390: the type option data.
L4391: 
L4392: IFieldTypeOptionLoad
L4393: 
L4394: Defines how to load a `Field`'s type option data. For example, when we create a
L4395: new `Field`, we use `NewTypeOptionLoader`. We use `FieldTypeOptionLoader` to load
L4396: the existing `Field`'s type option data.
L4397: 
L4398: FieldTypeOptionEditor
L4399: 
L4400: `FieldTypeOptionEditor` is a widget that provides a custom UI for each `Field`.
L4401: You can provide a custom UI by extending the `TypeOptionWidgetBuilder` As the
L4402: image below shows, we have many `TypeOptionWidgetBuilder` implementations.
L4403: 
L4404: The widget returned by `TypeOptionWidgetBuilder` use `TypeOptionWidgetContext` as
L4405: its data model. For example, `DateTypeOptionWidget` uses `DateTypeOptionContext`
L4406: that extends the `TypeOptionWidgetContext`.
L4407: 
L4408: `TypeOptionWidgetContext` uses `TypeOptionDataParser` to parse the generic data,
L4409: List, to specific data type. As the image below shows, each `TypeOptionContext`
L4410: must have a corresponding `TypeOptionDataParser`.

L4414: A `Row` represents a group of related `Cells`.

L4489: # Inter-Process Communication
L4490: 
L4491: AppFlowy uses a particular style of Inter-Process Communication called
L4492: Asynchronous Message Passing, where processes exchange requests and responses are
L4493: serialized using the Protobuf representation.
L4494: 
L4495: Message passing is a safer technique than shared memory or direct function access
L4496: because the recipient is free to reject or discard requests as it sees fit. For
L4497: example, if the Flowy Core determines a request is invalid, it simply discards
L4498: the requests and never executes the corresponding function. This article is going
L4499: to explain how the event process works.
L4500: 
L4501: ## Events
L4502: 
L4503: AppFlowy's backend defines all the events and generates the event's foreign
L4504: function interface. Currently, AppFlowy supports Dart and TS event call.
L4505: 
L4506: Events are emitted in the frontend and are processed in the backend. Each event
L4507: has its own handler in the backend. Each event can carry a payload that is
L4508: serialized using protobuf. This payload will be deserialized in the backend using
L4509: the corresponding protobuf struct.
L4510: 
L4511: Please check out this if you want to know the details of the events.
L4512: 
L4513: For example, using `UserEventSignIn` to trigger event with passed-in parameter in
L4514: the backend.
L4515: 
L4516: ```typescript
L4517: async function sendSignInEvent() {
L4518: let make_payload = () =>
L4519: SignInPayloadPB.fromObject({
L4520: email: nanoid(4) + "@gmail.com",
L4521: password: "A!@123abc",
L4522: name: "abc",
L4523: });
L4524: await UserEventSignIn(make_payload());
L4525: }
L4526: 
L4527: ```
L4528: 
L4529: ## Notifications
L4530: 
L4531: Notifications one-way messages that are best suited to communicate lifecycle
L4532: events and state changes. Notifications are triggered in the backend and received
L4533: in the frontend. Each notification can carry payload that is serialized using
L4534: protobuf. This payload will be deserialized in the frontend using the
L4535: corresponding protobuf struct.
L4536: 
L4537: For example, using `UserNotificationListener` to receive notifications when new
L4538: user signs in.
L4539: 
L4540: ```typescript
L4541: let listener = await new UserNotificationListener({
L4542: onUserSignIn: (userProfile) => {
L4543: console.log(userProfile);
L4544: },
L4545: onProfileUpdate(userProfile) {
L4546: console.log(userProfile);
L4547: // stop listening the changes
L4548: // listener.stop();
L4549: }}
L4550: );
L4551: 
L4552: listener.start();
L4553: 
L4554: ```

L4646: 
L4647: Below, you will find some quick definitions to help you read through the
L4648: document.
L4649: 
L4650: Database AppFlowy self-defined database that manages the relation between
L4651: columns, rows and cells.Grid A Grid type is a simple representation of items
L4652: placed in columns and rows.Board A Board is an project management tool designed
L4653: to help visualize work, limit work-in-progress.Calendar A Calendar allows you to
L4654: display data associated with dates and times in day, week or month formats.
